extracted.intended_audience: general newspaper readers interested in wartime reporting
extracted.subtask_description: Reporting and composing frontline/war dispatches for a general-audience newspaper, combining official communiqués, eyewitness diary entries, tactical details, and human-interest narrative. Emphasizes timeliness, attribution, and vivid on-scene description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness / 'first' reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Flag and promote being first with a development (example header: “First Invasion Report From Air”), and use timestamps to show contemporaneous reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include explicit time-of-observation entries (e.g., 4:46, 5:06), mark delayed dispatches when necessary (e.g., “May 11 (Delayed)”), and lead with notable firsts or breaking items to signal exclusivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of official communiqués and cited military sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Rely on and quote formal military communiqués and identified officials (e.g., “Allied Headquarters in Australia…”, “a Navy communique issued in Washington”, quotes from Generals and Colonels).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attribute operational claims and casualty/effectiveness statements to named units/communiqués; use official statements to anchor factual assertions and provide chain-of-command credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chronological diary / timestamped narrative
rubrics_metrics.description: Structure portions of the report as a time-stamped diary (minute/hour markers documenting actions and observations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use sequential time entries to convey tempo and immediacy (examples throughout: 4:48, 5:07, 8:00, 10:54), letting readers follow events as they unfolded; indicate when entries are retrospective or delayed.

rubrics_metrics.name: On-scene eyewitness detail and sensory description
rubrics_metrics.description: Incorporate vivid sensory details from observers (fog, smell of burned clothing, sounds of motors and shells, sights of fires and snow).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use concrete sensory language to convey atmosphere and make abstract military actions tangible; include small artifacts (e.g., orchid plant, pomades, tin-can dipper) to humanize and authenticate the scene.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attribution and caution about uncertainty
rubrics_metrics.description: Qualify information that is fragmentary or unconfirmed (phrases like “fragmentary radio bits indicate,” “informed sources who cannot be identified,” “report said”).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mark rumor vs. confirmed fact explicitly, avoid presenting unverified reports as definitive, and note source anonymity where applicable to preserve honesty about reliability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operational/tactical detail: locations, objectives, troop movements
rubrics_metrics.description: Report specific geographic and tactical information (named landing points, airdromes, passes, objectives such as Holtz Bay, Massacre Pass, Wewak; descriptions of three-pronged attacks and troop movements).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide place names, relative bearings/distances, and clear statements of objectives and maneuvers so readers understand what forces sought to accomplish and where engagements occurred.

rubrics_metrics.name: Casualty, equipment and ordnance reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Give counts and specifics for casualties, bombs dropped (e.g., “nineteen tons of bombs”), lost/saved men, captured materiel, and equipment performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supply numeric estimates where available (casualties, tons of bombs, number of planes), describe captured/abandoned equipment and supplies to illustrate material effects of operations; attribute figures to sources when uncertain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human-interest anecdotes and named individuals
rubrics_metrics.description: Include personal stories, named individuals, ranks and backgrounds (e.g., Captain Willoughby, Sergeant William Sherman) and their quotations to personalize the campaign.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Embed short profiles, direct quotes, and anecdotal incidents (heroic acts, hardships, small human moments) to connect readers emotionally and provide narrative hooks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logistics and material context
rubrics_metrics.description: Report on supply, clothing, food and packing practices (comparisons of Japanese and American clothing, packaging of rations, supply drops and failures).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain how logistics affect operations (e.g., clothing suitability, supply-drop timing, ration packaging), using concrete examples to illuminate strategic and human consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vivid narrative framing / striking lead
rubrics_metrics.description: Open with a clear, evocative lead sentence or image that frames the action (examples: descriptions of fires in marshalling yards, bombardment cascades).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin with an arresting fact or image to draw readers in, then expand into details; use the lead to set tone and scope of the dispatch.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of mixed formats within one dispatch
rubrics_metrics.description: Combine communiqué summaries, a diarist’s minute-by-minute notes, feature-style descriptive paragraphs, and analytical columns (e.g., 'What's Behind The War News').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Blend formats to provide immediate facts, on-the-ground texture, and broader analysis in one piece; clearly separate formats (communiqué vs. diary vs. commentary) to avoid confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographic orientation and measurement
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide distances, directions and spatial context (e.g., “325 miles up the New Guinea north coast,” “Amchitka to Kiska, 70 miles,” bearings relative to Darwin).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include distances and clear geographic references so readers can place events; use familiar reference points (cities, islands) and, when possible, numeric ranges to convey scale.
